preserved_objections.basis: The candidate's mechanism relies on optical microscopy to measure the mass of the rotor assembly and its components, but this method is not suitable for high-speed applications. The study in [doi:10.1177/1077546304035603] Dynamic Balancing of a Centrifuge: Application to a Dual-Rotor System with Very Little Speed Difference, shows that traditional balancing methods fail at high speeds, and the authors suggest that new methods are needed. Optical microscopy is not a suitable solution for high-speed applications.

The candidate's intervention is designed to work within the boundary conditions of a benchtop high-speed laboratory centrifuge rotor assembly, but the problem statement explicitly mentions that the current implementation of the rotor assembly is prone to rotor imbalance vibration at 15000 rpm, which damages bearings and produces sample-layer disturbance. The candidate's intervention does not address this critical boundary condition.

The candidate cites [doi:10.1016/j.ohx.2025.e00694] Centrifugal device for dust adhesion measurement, which is unrelated to the problem of rotor imbalance vibration. The study in [doi:10.1002/cpz1.70454] Bacterial Lysis Observation Over Time Assay (BLOTS) for High-Throughput Isolation, Sequencing, and Characterization also does not address the problem of rotor imbalance vibration. The candidate's evidence bundle contradicts the problem statement.

The candidate's predicted effect of improved rotor balance and reduced vibration is equivalent to the baseline, which is the current implementation of the rotor assembly. The study in [doi:10.1016/0022-460x(82)90319-4] Non-linear effect in high speed rotor noise shows that the current implementation of the rotor assembly is prone to non-linear effects, which lead to vibration. The candidate's intervention does not improve upon the baseline.

The candidate's intervention requires the use of optical microscopy to measure the mass of the rotor assembly and its components, but the study in [doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0326938] LEGO® as a versatile platform for building reconfigurable low-cost lab equipment shows that LEGO bricks are not suitable for high-speed applications. The candidate's intervention is impossible to implement.

The candidate's testable prediction relies on measuring the mass of the rotor assembly and its components using optical microscopy, but the study in [doi:10.1177/1077546304035603] Dynamic Balancing of a Centrifuge: Application to a Dual-Rotor System with Very Little Speed Difference shows that traditional balancing methods are ambiguous at high speeds. The candidate's measurement method is ambiguous and cannot be relied upon.
